reference.source: Williams Obstetrics / Novak's Gynecology / Campbell-Walsh Urology
clinicalPearls: Cord prolapse is descent of the umbilical cord below the presenting part after membrane rupture (overt) or alongside it with intact membranes (occult), threatening the fetal blood supply
It is an acute obstetric emergency because compression of the cord and reflex vasospasm rapidly cause fetal hypoxia and can lead to stillbirth if delivery is delayed
Predisposing factors include a high or poorly applied presenting part, malpresentation (breech, transverse, oblique), polyhydramnios, prematurity, multiple pregnancy, and long cord
Iatrogenic rupture of membranes when the presenting part is not engaged is a recognised trigger, so artificial rupture should be avoided with an unengaged head
The classic sign is an abrupt, severe fetal heart rate deceleration or bradycardia immediately after membrane rupture; a loop of cord may be palpable or visible at the introitus

Immediate management aims to relieve cord compression: elevate the presenting part manually or by filling the bladder, position the mother knee-chest or in steep head-down tilt, and minimise handling of an exposed cord to prevent vasospasm
Definitive treatment is the fastest safe delivery, usually emergency caesarean section, unless vaginal delivery is imminent and quicker
Tocolysis may buy time by reducing contractions while preparations for delivery are made
Outcome depends chiefly on the interval from diagnosis to delivery and on the setting, with the best results when it occurs in hospital with rapid theatre access
reference.pathophysiology: When the umbilical cord slips past the presenting part, it becomes trapped between the fetus and the maternal pelvis or lower uterine segment. Mechanical compression occludes the umbilical vessels, and exposure of the cord to cold air or handling induces vasospasm of the umbilical arteries. Both mechanisms interrupt oxygenated blood flow from the placenta to the fetus, producing acute fetal hypoxaemia, acidosis, and, if unrelieved, hypoxic-ischaemic injury or death. A poorly fitting presenting part leaves space for the cord to descend, which explains the association with malpresentation, prematurity, and polyhydramnios.
additionalDifferentials: Vasa praevia with fetal vessel rupture
Placental abruption causing acute fetal compromise
Cord compression from oligohydramnios (nuchal or true knot) without frank prolapse
Maternal supine hypotension causing transient fetal heart rate changes
additionalInvestigations: Continuous electronic fetal heart rate monitoring to detect bradycardia or variable decelerations
Vaginal examination to confirm a palpable pulsating cord and assess cervical dilatation and presenting part
Rapid bedside assessment of fetal viability
Ultrasound where time allows to confirm presentation and fetal heart activity
Preparation for theatre including maternal bloods and cross-match as part of emergency delivery
redFlags: OBSTETRIC EMERGENCY: sudden fetal bradycardia or profound decelerations after membrane rupture demanding immediate delivery
Visible or palpable pulsating cord at or beyond the introitus
Loss of cord pulsation suggesting critical fetal compromise
Malpresentation or unengaged presenting part with ruptured membranes
Any delay in achieving delivery once prolapse is confirmed
reference.prognosis: When cord prolapse is recognised promptly and delivery is expedited, particularly in a hospital setting, perinatal survival is good and long-term neurological outcomes are usually favourable. Prognosis worsens markedly with longer diagnosis-to-delivery intervals, out-of-hospital events, and prematurity, where hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy and perinatal death become more likely.
pitfalls: Performing artificial rupture of membranes with a high or unengaged presenting part
Excessive handling or attempts to replace an exposed cord, provoking vasospasm
Delaying transfer to theatre while arranging investigations
Failing to relieve cord compression by positioning or bladder filling while awaiting delivery
Not maintaining manual elevation of the presenting part during preparation for caesarean
management: Immediately relieve cord compression by manually elevating the presenting part, filling the bladder, and placing the mother in knee-chest or steep head-down position
Minimise handling of an exposed cord and keep it warm and moist to prevent umbilical artery vasospasm, avoiding attempts to replace it
Expedite delivery, by emergency caesarean section when vaginal birth is not imminent, or assisted vaginal delivery if the cervix is fully dilated and delivery is rapid
Stop oxytocin infusion and consider tocolysis to reduce contractions while preparing for delivery
Maintain continuous electronic foetal heart rate monitoring throughout
Summon urgent obstetric, anaesthetic and neonatal teams and prepare for neonatal resuscitation
Prevent recurrence by avoiding artificial rupture of membranes when the presenting part is high or unengaged
